title: Address to ZIP Code Lookup: ZCTA Explained
description: Find an address's ZIP code and see its Census ZCTA with Address to ZIP Code Lookup — the two are related, not identical. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, an address can carry one ZIP for mail while sitting inside a ZCTA built from the surrounding block group — the page shows both and explains the difference instead of hiding it.
quick_answer: Address to ZIP Code Lookup finds the postcode for a US address and shows it alongside the Census ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA) the address falls in, with the ZCTA's boundary and demographic context. Search and read both numbers — because for mail and statistics, they are cousins, not twins.
steps_intro: Two systems, two answers, both shown honestly:

body.t: Mail wants the USPS ZIP; analysis wants the ZCTA. Knowing which question you are answering is most of data hygiene — the county companion is
The ZCTA's ACS profile (population, income, housing) describes the neighbourhood statistically — the layer marketers and researchers actually use.
When two files disagree about an address's ZIP, the ZCTA comparison often reveals one of them was holding Census geography all along.
A lookup is not postal certification, but it catches the wrong-city and wrong-state errors before the postage is spent.
USPS ZIP codes are delivery routes, not areas — they can cross the ZCTA's tidy polygon without apologising. The page draws the ZCTA because that is the boundary statistics can stand on.
One address: a mailing ZIP from the postal world, a ZCTA from the Census world. Most days they match digit for digit; the days they do not are why this page exists.

faq: Does this verify that USPS will deliver to the address?
No. It finds the address's postal label and its Census ZCTA with context. Deliverability certification is USPS's own process; this is a lookup, honestly framed.
Why show both postcode and ZCTA?
Because users conflate them and datasets mix them. Showing both, labelled, ends the confusion at the source.
Does the map show an official USPS ZIP boundary?
No — USPS does not publish ZIP boundaries as areas. The polygon drawn is the Census ZCTA, labelled as such.
Can the two numbers differ?
Yes, at edges and in special cases (PO boxes, unique ZIPs). The page shows the pair so the difference is visible, not discovered later.
Can I use coordinates instead of an address?
Yes — a point works the same way: the ZCTA containing it, plus any mailing label the data associates.
What vintage is the context?
ACS estimates with their period stated in the tool — survey estimates, not a live count of your street.
ZIP codes outside the US?
This page is US-shaped. Other countries' postcode tools (UK, Canada) live elsewhere on the site in their own formats.
My ZIP has letters or a plus-four.
ZIP+4 refines the route further; this page works at the 5-digit and ZCTA level. Letters mean you are likely looking at a non-US system — the site's country tools handle those.
Why is my neighbourhood's ZCTA named by a different town?
ZCTAs take the name of the dominant place in the area, which can be the postal city next door. The number is the identity; the name is a label.
Do ZCTAs exist for PO-box ZIPs?
Not always — box-only ZIPs may have no ZCTA, one of the honest gaps this page surfaces instead of papering over.
Business or residential ZCTA?
ZCTAs describe all addresses in their blocks together. The ACS context mixes both, as real neighbourhoods do.
